title: Gnocchi Verdi
subtitle: Spinach and ricotta gnocchi with butter and Parmesan
excerpt: Gnocchi verdi are green gnocchi: the classic ricotta and spinach mixture shaped into small ovals. They are very close to gnudi and malfatti but formed more precisely. They are served with browned butter or a simple tomato sauce. They taste of spinach and ricotta and fresh pasta all at once.
sourceNotes: Green gnocchi (gnocchi verdi) are found across central Italy, particularly in Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna. They are closely related to gnudi and malfatti. The combination of spinach, ricotta, Parmesan, egg, and a little flour is one of the oldest fillings in Italian pasta cookery.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be refrigerated for up to 2 hours before cooking.

content.text: The technique is simple but needs careful draining: both the ricotta and the spinach must be very dry before they are mixed. A wet mixture produces soft, sticky dumplings that are hard to shape and may fall apart. Drain the ricotta in a sieve for at least 30 minutes; wring the spinach in a clean cloth until no more water comes out.

items.prepNote: well drained in a sieve for at least 30 minutes

content.text: Combine drained {{ricotta}} ricotta with finely chopped {{spinach-frozen}} spinach, {{parmesan}} Parmesan, {{eggs}} egg, {{nutmeg}} nutmeg, and {{salt-table}} salt. Add {{00-flour}} flour and mix gently until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Refrigerate for 30 minutes.
With floured hands, roll small portions of the dough into oval shapes about 4cm long. Place on a floured tray.
Cook in batches in well-salted boiling water until they float and have been at the surface for 30 seconds. Lift with a slotted spoon.
Brown {{unsalted-butter}} butter in a wide pan over medium heat until golden. Add {{sage}} sage leaves and crisp for 30 seconds. Add the gnocchi and toss gently. Serve with more Parmesan.

items.symptom: The gnocchi are heavy and dense
items.cause: Too much flour, or the spinach and ricotta were wet.
items.fix: Add the minimum flour needed to bring the dough together. If the ricotta and spinach are properly dry, you need very little. Wet ingredients require more flour, which makes the gnocchi heavy.

content.text: Green gnocchi are found across Tuscany, Emilia-Romagna, and Umbria. The combination of spinach, ricotta, Parmesan, egg, and nutmeg is the canonical Italian pasta filling, adapted here into a free-form dumpling rather than enclosed in pasta. In Tuscany they are often called gnudi; in Emilia they are malfatti. The browned butter and sage dressing is shared with the potato gnocchi and stuffed pasta traditions of northern Italy.
